extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, patent prosecutors, and federal judges (practitioners in patent litigation)
extracted.subtask_description: Appellate (Federal Circuit) guidance on standards for JMOL, anticipation, and the printed-matter doctrine as applied to asserted patent claims. Focuses on when prior art anticipates claims, when informational markings are patentable weight, and how evidentiary admissions/stipulations affect JMOL.

rubrics_metrics.name: JMOL legal standard
rubrics_metrics.description: JMOL is appropriate if 'a reasonable jury would not have a legally sufficient evidentiary basis to find for [the nonmoving party] on [the issue].' (FED. R. CIV. P. 50(a)(1))
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the regional circuit's law for review of a district court's grant of JMOL (here Third Circuit); determine whether, viewing the full evidentiary record, any reasonable jury could have had a legally sufficient basis to find for the nonmoving party. If not, JMOL is warranted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard of appellate review (fact v. law)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a claim is directed to printed matter (patent-eligibility) is a question of law reviewed de novo; anticipation is a question of fact reviewed for substantial evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deferential review (substantial evidence) applies to factual findings about anticipation—i.e., ask whether the record contains 'such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support a conclusion.' Legal questions (e.g., printed matter as a §101 issue) get de novo review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requirement (claim elements in prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated when a single prior art reference (or product) discloses every limitation of the asserted claim such that the prior art 'anticipates' the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art products that sometimes embody the claimed characteristics can still anticipate (citing Hewlett-Packard Co. v. Mustek Sys.); use stipulations, admissions, expert testimony, studies, lab notebooks, and exhibits to determine whether each claim limitation is present in the prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed-matter doctrine (informational content lacks patentable weight)
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of information conveyed by claimed markers (e.g., that a port is suitable for certain pressures/flow) is 'printed matter' not entitled to patentable weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limitations that merely claim informational content (mental steps to recognize printed matter) do not add patentable weight. Use cases like Praxair and prior Federal Circuit precedent to determine when limitations are merely printed matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: When a marking/marker gets patentable weight (structure vs content)
rubrics_metrics.description: A radiographic marker is entitled to patentable weight only to the extent it constitutes a structural feature that is radiographically discernible, not because of any meaning ascribed to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between (1) informational content of a marking (printed matter — no weight) and (2) the physical/structural means by which information is conveyed (may be given weight if it is a structural, radiographically discernible feature). Evaluate whether the claimed advance focuses on the content or the means of conveyance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters/typographical markings are ordinarily printed matter
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed 'radiographic letter' (e.g., radiographic letters etched on a port) is printed matter because a letter intrinsically conveys typographical meaning and is not functionally related to the substrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent evidence of a technical/functional effect arising from using a letter (as opposed to other indicia), typographical markings should be treated as informational printed matter and not used to distinguish over prior art (citing In re Marco Guldenaar Holding B.V.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental-step limitations implicate printed matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim limitations that require a user to recognize or mentally process information (mental steps) may attempt to capture informational content and thus be considered printed matter lacking patentable weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim's limitation consists of 'identifying' information on an x-ray (or similar recognition), analyze whether that step merely recites a mental recognition of printed matter; if so, it does not confer patentable weight (citing Praxair).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary weight of admissions and stipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Stipulations and expert admissions (e.g., that titanium ports were radiographically visible before a priority date or that some prior ports 'pass' power-injection testing) can constitute uncontested evidence that forecloses reasonable dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When admissions/stipulations, corroborated by exhibits (x-rays, lab notebooks, studies), establish a claim limitation in prior art, a court may properly conclude there is no genuine dispute of material fact for a jury, supporting JMOL.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of claim-language requirement is dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: If a purported distinguishing feature (e.g., FDA approval for a particular use) is not required by the claim language or the claim construction, then lack of that feature in the prior art does not mean the prior art fails to anticipate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not import requirements (like regulatory approval) into claim scope when the claim text and construction do not include them; anticipation is assessed against the claim as properly construed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctiveness/identifiability via imaging as a factual inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'identifiable feature' or 'radiographic marker' can be satisfied by a radiographically discernible attribute such as port shape; whether a port's shape is 'readily identifiable' via x-ray is a factual determination informed by expert testimony and image exhibits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If experts agree (or evidence shows) that a prior-art product has discernible shape/features on x-ray, that can satisfy the 'identifiable feature' limitation as a matter of law where the evidentiary record is uncontroverted.
